newsitem.title: UK: Dlr rises as Buba refrains from springing surprise.
newsitem.headline: Dlr rises as Buba refrains from springing surprise.

text.p: The dollar rose, climbing to within a quarter-pfennig of the multi-year highs it set against the mark on Monday, after the Bundesbank did not spring any surprises at its weekly money-market transactions.
Speculation that the German central bank could engineer higher money-market rates had intensified as the mark slumped to a near-eight-year low of 1.8730 yesterday.

Traders had focused on the possibility that the Bundesbank would call for a variable-rate tender alongside the expected fixed-rate tender. Such talk had driven the dollar nearly 1.5 pfennigs off its peaks against the mark overnight.
The dollar rebounded as these concerns proved unfounded, and is expected by analysts to extend its gains in coming days.

"Dollar/mark will soon be testing new highs given the Bundesbank has done nothing today and that it will be another week before we find out what they are going to do about rates," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International.
The dollar was at 1.8701/06 marks at 0750 GMT from 1.8618 late on Monday in New York. It was at 118.54/64 yen from 118.06 yesterday.
German interest rate expectations and trading in dollar/mark are now seen taking their cue from economic data.
The perception that German economic recovery is still too fragile to withstand a sharp rise in interest rates has encouraged traders to push the mark down.
The German currency has fallen 7.7 percent against the dollar since the beginning of July and is at five-year lows in trade-weighted terms.
Also contributing to the mark's decline against the dollar has been the contrast presented by the strength of U.S. growth.
"In the current environment it is just so easy to latch on to factors that work towards mark selling," said Junpei Yamamoto, head of foreign exchange at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
"The market now has 1.90 in its sights."
Traders are looking to the July German jobless report released tomorrow and June new manufacturing orders data due out this week for an incentive to drive the mark even lower.
Stronger-than-expected reports would stoke talk of an increase in the repo rate as early as next week and help to bolster the mark, at least in the short-term, analysts said.

Strong data "would help the mark a little and the knee-jerk reaction to a rate rise will be to buy marks," said Julian Jessop, European analyst at Nikko Europe. "But the mark will then continue to weaken because of EMU."

Expectations have grown this year that European economic and monetary union will be launched by a broad group of countries and that the entry criteria will not be interpreted as strictly as previously expected.
Such expectations were stoked after the Ifo research institute predicted on Monday that Germany's budget deficit will be 3.3 percent of its gross domestic product in 1997.

While this is above the three percent reference rate required of EMU entrants by the Maastricht treaty, Ifo said it would not necessarily be too high to prevent Germany from qualifying for EMU from the outset.
